summary:
Norte de Santander stands under Colombia's national framework, which is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on self-recognition without a surgical requirement; marriage equality has been available since 2016, adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025. A comprehensive trans law remained under legislative consideration in 2025.

Courts have also intervened directly in custody, ruling on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty and protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.

The enforcement gap is severe. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025. The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, welcoming the government's legal reforms while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected and that killings are rising.

Lethal anti-trans violence has occurred in daylight and on film. Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in Bello, Antioquia on 4 April 2025; the assault was filmed and the video went viral on 5 April, and she died of cardiac arrest that afternoon. Police interrogated local residents but no one had been arrested even after President Petro ordered an urgent investigation. Her mother Sandra Borja stated, "They killed her for being who she was". One report counted 13 trans people killed by hate in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025.

Where armed groups operate, the risk takes an organised form. In Caquetá department, armed groups ran a "social cleansing" campaign whose flyers, circulated on the streets and via WhatsApp, named "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets. A trans woman and local election candidate was told by three armed men she had one week to leave town, hid for a week, then fled at night; a second trans woman said a friend had been killed. In Guajira department, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals under the wording "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". Nationally, eight trans women were killed between February and April 2024 and 41 in 2023, and discrimination confines trans women in these departments mainly to hairdressing or sex work.

Some of this violence has been prosecuted as an international crime. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against them constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity. The UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern.

No Norte de Santander-specific legal, enforcement or incident finding appears in the sourced material, and no deviation from the national position is material enough to score separately. The department does sit in the country's frontier belt, where "orden público" regimes mean armed groups rather than departmental police effectively regulate conduct, and Caribe Afirmativo's 2025 report documents the territorial expansion of violence alongside an insufficient state response, with trans women displaced from such departments because of their gender identity by the same armed actors that displace others.
tangentialFactors:
The violence recorded in the sources operates through two distinct mechanisms that a visitor should not conflate. One is opportunistic urban assault: the attack on Sara Millerey in Bello occurred in daylight, was filmed by bystanders, and produced no arrest despite a presidential order for investigation. The other is organised territorial control, in which armed groups publish lists, set deadlines and enforce them, as in Caquetá and Guajira. Norte de Santander belongs to the second pattern through its frontier status and the presence of "orden público" regimes.

The prosecution route has also diverged from ordinary homicide. The Special Jurisdiction for Peace's July 2023 indictment recast conflict-driven attacks on LGBT people as gender persecution, a crime against humanity, which places some of the same conduct outside ordinary criminal processing altogether.

Reported national totals differ by source and period: the Attorney General's Office logged 35 LGBTI murders from January to May 2025, one report counted 13 trans people killed by hate in the first quarter of 2025, and other tallies give 41 trans women killed in 2023 and eight between February and April 2024. These figures are not reconcilable into a single series and should be read as separate counts with separate methodologies.

Economic narrowing compounds the physical risk. In the departments where armed-group campaigns are documented, discrimination leaves trans women limited mainly to hairdressing or sex work, and sex work in turn concentrates them in the spaces where threats are delivered.
localsOnly:
Colombian residents change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, a route open since the June 2015 rule change; no judicial order, bodily inspection or psychiatric assessment is required. Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 grounds recognition in self-recognition without a surgical requirement.

Same-sex couples have been able to marry since 2016 and to adopt since 2015. From November 2025 national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers.

Residents deprived of liberty have direct court protection: a Colombian court has ruled on the treatment of a trans woman in custody and on the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.

A comprehensive trans law was still before the legislature in 2025, so protections continue to rest on constitutional jurisprudence, administrative rules and individual court rulings rather than a single statute.

Residents in armed-group-controlled departments face threats delivered through flyers and WhatsApp, deadlines to leave town, and displacement on grounds of gender identity. Caribe Afirmativo's 2025 report records trans women displaced from frontier departments by the same armed actors that displace other residents, alongside an insufficient state response.
